results.title: Field Notes: The AgentCore Memory write that returns success and reads back empty
results.summary:
# Summary

The author discovered two operational gotchas when using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore's long-term memory: a non-existent API method (`ingest_memory_records`) that passed code review but would fail at runtime, and a critical read-after-write consistency issue where `BatchCreateMemoryRecords` returns `201` success but the record remains unsearchable in its namespace for 15-30 seconds despite being immediately readable by ID. The post provides practical guidance on verifying SDK operations exist, understanding the distinction between direct namespace writes and semantic indexing, and implementing proper polling strategies instead of fixed delays.
results.reasoning: The summary accurately captures the two main issues (non-existent API and read-after-write delay), correctly states the 15-30 second lag from the measured data, distinguishes between ID-based and namespace-based reads, and reflects the practical guidance provided without adding unsupported claims.

results.title: Every dashboard was green while the agent burned six figures a year
results.summary:
# Summary

This post describes a costly failure mode where an AI agent ran in an infinite loop for days without triggering any traditional monitoring alerts, because standard dashboards track uptime and errors rather than token consumption and tool calls. The author outlines five specific conditions that cause agent runaways (context bloat, unsatisfiable goals, model regeneration, broken tools, and external re-drives), then recommends both hard iteration caps to stop runaway loops and custom per-session and fleet-level instrumentation to catch them before they become expensive.
results.reasoning: The summary accurately captures the main failure mode (invisible runaway loop), the five specific conditions causing runaways, and the two-part solution (hard caps and custom instrumentation at both per-session and fleet levels), all directly supported by the source.

results.title: The LLM is not a security boundary
results.summary: This post explains how to architect an AI agent system that safely handles sensitive data by treating the language model as fundamentally untrustworthy and building deterministic security controls around it rather than relying on prompts. The author argues that effective security requires multiple ranked layers of defense—each with known vulnerabilities—stacked so that no single failure exposes protected data, with deterministic controls closest to the data and probabilistic safeguards as an outer backstop.
results.reasoning: The summary accurately captures the post's core thesis about treating the LLM as untrusted, implementing deterministic controls in code rather than prompts, and using defense-in-depth with ranked layers where each has known holes but no single failure reaches the data.

results.title: Your LLM security diagram defends the wrong layer
results.summary:
# Summary

The post argues that the standard LLM security architecture diagram—which maps four attack types (prompt injection, retrieval poisoning, context poisoning, output injection) to probabilistic defenses at each stage—defends the wrong layer. Instead, security should rely on a deterministic boundary at the point where model output becomes action (tool calls, database queries, etc.), where an enumerable set of allowed actions can be checked against a verified principal, rather than attempting to classify infinite attack variations upstream.
results.reasoning: The summary accurately captures the post's central argument about the standard diagram defending the wrong layer, the proposed solution of deterministic boundaries at action points, and the key distinction between enumerating allowed actions versus classifying attacks, with all claims directly supported by the source.

results.title: Part 1: Intent vs State. How AWS DevOps Agent Closes the Gap Between What Your System Is and What You Decided It Should Be
results.summary:
# Summary

This post introduces a gap in current AI agent capabilities: while agents can read documentation and call APIs, they struggle to correlate real-time system state with organizational decisions (like risk acceptances or architectural commitments). The author describes building an AWS DevOps Agent system that combines telemetry monitoring with a searchable knowledge base of ADRs, runbooks, and planning documents—using structured YAML frontmatter as the contract—so that incidents can be understood in context of past decisions, not just recent changes. The series will walk through the architecture, the MCP layer for querying organizational knowledge, and integration with AWS DevOps Agent.
results.reasoning: The summary accurately captures the main gap (agents can't correlate state with organizational decisions), the solution (AWS DevOps Agent + knowledge base with structured frontmatter), and the series structure, all directly supported by the source.

results.title: Part 1: Why I Chose Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (And What Lambda Gets Wrong for AI Agents)
results.summary:
# Summary

This post explains why the author chose Amazon Bedrock AgentCore over Lambda for building a production AI agent on AWS, detailing how Lambda's 15-minute timeout, stateless design, and lack of built-in session management make it poorly suited for conversational AI with persistent memory and long-running tool chains. AgentCore provides managed container orchestration specifically designed for stateful agent sessions, handling session routing, memory persistence, and streaming responses—though it requires understanding new abstractions and has a rougher developer experience than Lambda. The post introduces a multi-part series documenting the full production architecture, from CDK infrastructure and Python agent development to CI/CD pipelines and cost optimization.
results.reasoning: The summary accurately captures the main argument (AgentCore vs Lambda), key technical details (15-minute timeout, stateless design, session management), AgentCore's benefits (managed container orchestration, session routing, memory persistence, streaming), trade-offs (rougher developer experience), and the series structure, all directly supported by the source.

results.title: Part 2: The MCP Server: Turning ADRs and Incidents into a Queryable Org-Knowledge Surface

The approach trades one additional round trip per query for cost savings, freshness, filtering capability, and precise citations compared to embedding all documents in the system prompt.
results.reasoning: The summary accurately captures the main point (MCP server as typed query layer vs prompt-stuffing), the four-tool structure, the metadata-as-contract design, and the key trade-off (round trip for cost/freshness/filtering/precision), all directly supported by the source.
